Wrestle
RES-ul
v.
From Old English wræstlian, “to wrestle, struggle.” Renders the Hebrew ’ābaq, “to wrestle” (the rare verb used only of Jacob at Peniel), and the Greek noun palē, “wrestling” (used only of the Christian’s combat in Eph 6:12).

📖 Biblical Definition

Wrestling, in Scripture, names two great combats: the night-long contending of Jacob with the Angel of the LORD at Peniel, and the spiritual warfare of the saint against principalities and powers, world-rulers of this darkness, and wicked spirits in heavenly places. Genesis 32: Jacob, alone at the brook Jabbok the night before he is to meet Esau, is met by a Man with whom he wrestles until the breaking of the day; the Man touches the hollow of his thigh and puts it out of joint; Jacob will not let Him go until He blesses him; the Man names him Israel, for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed; and Jacob calls the place Peniel, for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved. Out of that wrestling Jacob walks limping the rest of his days—and changed forever. The story is the great Old Testament parable of the soul’s holy contending with God in prayer: pressing the promise, refusing to let go, being broken in the wrestling, and emerging blessed, named, and lame. Ephesians 6 names the other wrestling: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. The Christian is in a real, unseen, hand-to-hand combat with invisible powers; the whole armor of God is given for it; and the means of standing in the evil day are the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit, and prayer in the Spirit at all seasons. Wrestling therefore has both its inward face (the saint’s pleading and pressing with God in prayer) and its outward face (the church’s warfare against the unseen powers that contend for the souls of men). Both are arduous; neither is metaphor; and both are credentialed by the New Testament as part of the regular discipline of every saint.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WRESTLE as to strive with arms extended, to throw the antagonist; to struggle; to strive, contend; in scripture, to contend in prayer or in spiritual conflict.

expand to see more

WRESTLE, v.i. — 1. To strive with arms extended, as two men, who seize each other by the collar and arms, each endeavoring to throw the other. 2. To struggle; to strive; to contend; as, to wrestle with difficulties; to wrestle with temptations. 3. In scripture, to contend in prayer with great earnestness; to strive in spiritual conflict (Eph 6:12).

WRESTLING, n. — The act of striving to throw an antagonist; struggling; contention in prayer or spiritual conflict.

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 32:24-26 — "And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh... And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."

Ephesians 6:12 — "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."

Colossians 4:12 — "Epaphras... saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God."

Romans 15:30 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, for the Lord Jesus Christ’s sake, and for the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Wrestling is corrupted by the metaphorization of the age, which has reduced ‘wrestling with doubt’ or ‘wrestling with the text’ to a posture of intellectual sophistication that prides itself on never resolving anything—and by the parallel evaporation of the doctrine of real spiritual warfare against actual unseen powers.

expand to see more

The contemporary church has metaphorized wrestling beyond recognition. Wrestling with the text, wrestling with doubt, wrestling with my faith—the language is everywhere, but its content has hollowed. Where Jacob wrestled with God and was changed, where Epaphras labored fervently in prayer that the saints might stand complete, where Paul charged the Romans to strive together with me in your prayers, the modern wrestler often poses rather than contends: the wrestling becomes a posture of intellectual sophistication that prides itself on the wrestling and is suspicious of any actual resolution. The biblical pattern is the opposite. Jacob wrestled all night and would not let go until he was blessed; the wrestling was means, not end; the blessing was sought and obtained. Recover the pattern, and wrestling in prayer becomes again what it is in the Bible: a real holy contending with God for the promised blessing, by a soul that intends not to leave the wrestling without the answer.

Wrestling is also corrupted by the parallel evaporation of the doctrine of real spiritual warfare. Ephesians 6 is read as figurative encouragement rather than as the apostle’s plain assertion that the church is in a hand-to-hand combat with actual unseen powers, and that the armor of God is provided precisely because the combat is real. The result is a Christianity that takes neither face of biblical wrestling seriously: it does not contend with God in prayer for the blessing, and it does not contend with the powers of darkness in spiritual warfare for the souls of men and the standing of the church. Recover both. Be Jacob at Peniel; be Paul in his prayer-labors for the churches; be Epaphras laboring fervently. The blessing is given to wrestlers who do not let go.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ’ābaq (to wrestle—only at Peniel) and Greek palē (wrestling—only in Eph 6:12): the saint’s holy contending with God in prayer and the church’s real warfare against unseen powers.

expand to see more

Hebrew ’ābaq (H79) — to wrestle; the rare verb used only of Jacob’s wrestling at Peniel.

Greek palē (G3823) — wrestling, struggle, combat; used only in Eph 6:12 of spiritual warfare.

Greek agōnizōmai (G75) — to contend, strive, agonize; used of Epaphras’s prayer-wrestling in Col 4:12.

Greek sunagōnizōmai (G4865) — to strive together with—Paul’s appeal in Rom 15:30.

Usage

"Wrestling has two great faces in Scripture: the saint’s holy contending with God in prayer, and the church’s combat against unseen principalities and powers."

"Jacob walked limping the rest of his days—the wrestling broke him and blessed him both, as it always does."

"Metaphorized ‘wrestling with doubt’ that never resolves is not biblical wrestling; Jacob would not let go until he was blessed."
